attributes.reason: Tink provides an open banking platform with extensive connectivity to European financial institutions similar to Plaid's core data aggregation service.
TrueLayer operates an open banking network that facilitates secure account access and payments, mirroring Plaid's functionality.
Galileo offers a financial technology platform that provides APIs for banking and payments, enabling companies to build fintech solutions.
Moov provides a comprehensive payments platform via API, allowing developers to integrate money movement services similarly to Plaid's payment APIs.
Yodlee is a direct competitor in the financial data aggregation space, providing APIs to connect and analyze consumer-permissioned financial data.
MX specializes in consumer-permissioned financial data aggregation and analytics, helping fintechs and financial institutions build better user experiences.
Salt Edge provides a global open banking gateway for data aggregation and payment initiation, directly competing with Plaid's service portfolio.
Yapily offers an open banking API platform that enables developers to access financial data and initiate payments, mirroring Plaid's core offering.
Flinks provides an embedded finance platform that unifies financial data connectivity and payment initiation for fintech applications.
Belvo is an open finance platform that provides APIs for data aggregation and payments, serving as the functional equivalent to Plaid in Latin American markets.
Akoya provides a secure API-based network for financial data sharing between institutions and fintech apps, focusing on the same data aggregation space.
Bud provides tools for financial institutions to access and enrich transactional data through open banking connectivity.
Brankas is an open finance technology provider that offers APIs for banking data and payment integration across Southeast Asia.
Lean Technologies provides financial infrastructure for data aggregation and payments in the Middle East, functioning as a regional peer to Plaid.
Fabrick enables open banking and payment services, allowing businesses to integrate financial features through a unified API platform.
Setu provides an API-first approach to financial services in India, enabling data access and payment initiation for developers.
Stripe provides broad financial infrastructure that includes payment processing and bank account connectivity APIs which overlap with Plaid's ecosystem.
Dwolla provides a sophisticated API layer for bank transfers and payment orchestration, competing in the infrastructure space for fintechs.
Unit is a banking-as-a-service platform that helps software companies embed financial features like accounts and payments into their applications.
Swan provides an API-based platform to embed banking services, including accounts and cards, into non-financial applications.

You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B benchmark.

Definition - a company lookalike API takes a seed company and returns other
companies that resemble it: by product, market, technology, or business
model. Teams use the results to expand an Ideal Customer Profile, build
prospecting lists, or find competitors and comparables.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company - the company the lookalike search started from.
  • A CANDIDATE company - a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide whether the CANDIDATE genuinely resembles the SEED under that
definition - a company that works as a competitor, comparable, or
ICP-expansion prospect for someone targeting companies like the SEED.

Rules:
  - relevant = true when the candidate's primary product/service carries the
    resemblance on at least one definitional axis, judged strictly:
      • product - sells essentially the same kind of product/service;
      • market - serves the same customer/buyer persona for the same job
        to be done, as a peer (not as a supplier or client of the seed);
      • business model - an equivalent model in the seed's space, such that
        the two are genuine competitors or comparables.
    The strongest lookalikes clear several axes at once; one axis held
    strongly is enough, one axis held weakly is not.
  - A shared generic taxonomy label or keyword is not enough. A similar
    technology stack alone is not enough either - technology co-signals
    support a product/market/model resemblance but cannot substitute for one.
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. Those are not benchmark
    constraints: a smaller or larger company can be a relevant lookalike.
    Ignore any such metadata in the candidate record when deciding relevance.
  - relevant = false for unrelated industries, parent companies,
    customers/clients of the seed, agencies/consultancies that serve the
    category (rather than competing), and parody/duplicate entries.
  - When in doubt, label false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words.

Examples:
  - HubSpot ↔ a smaller CRM/marketing-automation platform: true.
  - HubSpot ↔ a lead-generation agency using HubSpot for clients: false.
  - Shopify ↔ an online-store/e-commerce platform: true.
  - Shopify ↔ a payment processor with no storefront platform: false.

  - Datadog ↔ a generic IT consulting firm: false.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ an endpoint-security platform: true.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ a general-purpose IT monitoring tool with no security product: false.
  - Procore ↔ construction project-management software: true.
  - Procore ↔ a construction contractor: false.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ field-service management software for trades businesses: true.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ a plumbing company that uses field-service software: false.
  - Teladoc ↔ a virtual-care/telehealth platform: true.
  - Teladoc ↔ a health-insurance carrier with no telehealth product: false.
  - Veeva ↔ life-sciences CRM or clinical-operations software: true.
  - Veeva ↔ a generic CRM with no life-sciences focus: false.
  - Datadog ↔ a company running a similar cloud stack but selling HR software: false.
  - Nubank ↔ a digital bank operating in a different region: true.
